Sinninghe Damsté; Patrice Baby Abstract: This article presents new biostratigraphic dating, facies analysis, organic geochemical data and Nd-Sr isotopic provenance from five outcrops of southern Amazonia (MD-85, MD-177 MD-184, MD-255 and MD-256) to document for the first time the presence of a shallow marine ingression in the Paleocene of southern Amazonia basin. The co-occurrence of a selachian assemblage encompassing Potobatis sp., Ouledia sp., and Pristidae indet. with the ostracod Protobuntonia sp. and the charophytes Peckichara cf. varians meridionalis, Platychara perlata, and Feistiella cf. gildemeisteri suggests a Paleocene age for the studied deposits (most likely Thanetian but potentially Danian). Fifteen facies have been recognized and have been grouped into three facies assemblages. Facies association A corresponds to the sedimentary filling of a tide-influenced meandering channel formed in the fluvialtidal transition zone. Facies association B is related to more distal tidal-flats, little channelized tidal inlets and saltmarshes deposits. Facies association C corresponds to a stressed shallow marine environment such as a bay or a lagoon. The δ13CTOC value (-23.4 ‰) of MD-184 is enriched in 13C compared to the other samples suggesting the presence of substantial amounts of marine organic matter in MD-184. The δ13CTOC values of samples from other outcrops (-27.3 to -29.8 ‰) indicate a mixed organic matter origin, from terrestrial to brackish environments. The analyzed sediments have similar Nd-Sr isotopic compositions as those of the Cenozoic sediments of the Altiplano (εNd(0) values from -6.2 to -10.7 and 87Sr/86Sr compositions from 0.712024 to 0.719026) indicating a similar volcanic source. This multidisciplinary dataset documents the presence of a tide-dominated estuary sourced by the proto Western Cordillera debouching into a shallow marine bay during Paleocene times. This transgression might be explained by subsidence created in response to the proto-Western Cordillera loading. Similar to Miocene marine incursions affecting the Pebas megawetland, Paleogene marine incursions in the Amazonian foreland basin associated with Andean uplift may have played a role in the Neotropical biodiversity dynamics in favouring biogeographical isolation and promoting allopatric speciation for terrestrial organisms.

1. Introduction 48

The Amazon basin is the world’s largest Cenozoic fluvial basin with an actual drainage 49

area of 5.8×106 km2 and a depositional area of approximately 2.5 to 3×106 km2. The Amazon 50

rainforest, with an area of about 5.6×106 km2, is the largest rainforest ecosystem, representing 51

nearly 50% of the total tropical rainforest area on Earth. The Amazon rainforest plays a 52

significant role in global climate, the carbon cycle and biodiversity and is the most species- 53

rich terrestrial ecosystem in the world. However, the timing of the origin and evolutionary 54

causes of this diversity are still highly debated. A recent synthesis by Hoorn et al. (2010) has 55

highlighted the complex links between Andean mountain building, climate variability and 56

biodiversity development throughout Cenozoic times in the Amazonian basin. In particular 57

the occurrence of inland seaway is important not only in promoting biogeographical isolation 58

and allopatric speciation but also in controlling the precipitation rates in the Amazon basin 59

(Jeffery et al., 2012). Consequently, determining the number, timing and duration of Cenozoic 60

marine incursions recorded in Amazonian basin is fundamental not only for reconstructing 61

paleo-Amazonian landscapes and ecosystems through time but also for understanding the 62

close relationships between Andean mountain building and the Cenozoic climate and biotic 63

evolution of South America. 64

Several marine incursions have already been described in the Cenozoic sedimentary 65

record of the Amazonian foreland basins (Roddaz et al., 2010). For instance, the existence and 66

persistence of the early to middle Miocene Pebas megawetland system in northern Amazonia 67

is thought to have promoted the high biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest (for a review, see 68

(Hoorn et al., 2010) and references therein). However, the extent of this Pebas system and the 69

number of marine ingressions that have occurred is still under debate (Campbell et al., 2006; 70

Hovikoski et al., 2007; Hoorn et al., 2010) mainly because of poor stratigraphic dating and the 71

lack of regional data integration. In comparison, few studies document Paleogene marine 72

incursions in the Amazonian basin. For instance, there is some evidence of a marine 73

ingression during Eocene to Oligocene times in Colombia (Santos et al., 2008), Ecuador 74

(Christophoul et al., 2002) and northern Peru (Hermoza et al., 2005b), but no data exist for 75

earlier marine incursions. 76

In this study, new biostratigraphical, sedimentological and geochemical data are presented to 77

highlight a Paleocene marine ingression in southern Peru, Madre de Dios basin. A new paleo- 78

and paleo-extension of this shallow marine ingression are discussed. 80

2. Geological background 81

2.1. Paleocene sedimentary record in the Amazonian foreland basins 82

In nearly all the Central Andean sedimentary basins, late Eocene to early Oligocene 83

times are marked by a widespread sedimentary hiatus (Mpodozis and Allmendinger, 1993; 84

Marocco et al., 1995) corresponding to a major tectonic phase primarily called Incaic 1 phase 85

(Noble et al., 1990; Jaillard, 1996; Hermoza, 2004). However, there are some localities in 86

northern and Central Andean foreland basins where Paleocene strata have been preserved and 87

can be described (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). 88

In central Colombia, the Cuervos formation is late Paleocene in age (Jaramillo and 89

Dilcher, 2000; 2001) and its sedimentary rocks correspond to mudstones deposited in a distal 90

alluvial to coastal plain environment, in a foredeep position (Cooper et al., 1995; Parra et al., 91

2009). In the Putumayo basin of southern Colombia, the Rumiyaco Formation is barren of 92

fossils and then remains poorly constrained but it is assumed that it is early Paleocene in age. 93

The Rumiyaco Formation unconformably overlays the Cretaceous series and builts up a 94

sedimentary wedge onlapping onto older strata and disappearing toward the east of the basin. 95

The formation is characterized by possibly marine-related to mostly continental fine-grained 96

deposits in the western part of the Putumayo basin and evolves eastward into continental 97

sandstones (Bejarano, 1991; Casero, 1997; Córdoba et al., 1997; Londoño et al., 2012). In the 98

Ecuadorian Oriente basin, Paleocene strata dated by charophytes (Faucher and Savoyat, 1973) 99

are represented by the deposits of the fluvial Tena Formation. Various studies demonstrated 100

that sediments from Tena Formation are derived from the Eastern Cordillera of Ecuador (Ruiz 101

et al., 2004, 2007; Martin-Gombojav and Winkler, 2008). 102

In Peru, Paleocene strata are very scarce and are only identified in the eastern border 103

of the Altiplano (Vilquechico Group and Lower Muñani Formation), in the Cusco-Sicuani 104

2.2. Stratigraphy and structure of the Madre de Dios basin 120

The Madre de Dios basin is part of the southern Amazonian foreland basins system 121

(Roddaz et al., 2005). The Madre de Dios foreland basin is located northeastward to the 122

Eastern Cordillera (EC) of southern Peru and can be subdivided into the Sub-Andean Zone 123

(SAZ) and the Madre de Dios plain tectonomorphic units (Fig. 1-B) (Gil, 2001; Hermoza, 124

2004). The SAZ is characterized by both sedimentary filling and active deformation. In the 125

SAZ, propagation of deformation towards the Madre de Dios plain is controlled by the 126

development of deep duplexes, whose shortening is accommodated in surface by imbricates 127

and by the Sub-Andean thrust front. The Sub-Andean thrust front corresponds to the eastern 128

8

border of the SAZ and is responsible for transportation of a piggy-back basin, which outcrops 129

as a large syncline called Salvación syncline in the study area (Fig. 1-B). The deformed and 130

still active SAZ only corresponds to the internal (western) part of Madre de Dios foreland 131

basin. The external (eastern) part of the basin is situated east to the Sub-Andean thrust front 132

and corresponds to the non-deformed part of the system, the Madre de Dios plain. In this 133

study, we will only focus on outcropping strata from the Salvación syncline, in the SAZ of 134

Madre de Dios basin. 135

Upper Cretaceous to Cenozoic strata in Salvación piggy-back basin consist of +/- 4500 136

m of an alternance of marine, tide-influenced and fluvial deposits (Gil, 2001; Hermoza, 137

2004). Because of the very scarce outcrops, fauna and palynomorph material available in the 138

studied area, the general chronostratigraphy of this succession is quite difficult to assess and 139

many interrogations subsist for the Cretaceous-Paleogene interval (Gil, 2001; Hermoza, 140

2004), while Miocene deposits are much better constrained in terms of biochronology and 141

chronostratigraphy (Marivaux et al., 2012; Antoine et al., 2013; Antoine et al., Submitted). 142

Paleogene strata in the Salvación series and more broadly in the Madre de Dos basin are 143

supposed to correspond to the fluvial Huayabamba or the Red beds Formation. 144

3. Methodology 145

In the Madre de Dios basin, Paleogene deposits crop out along the Alto Madre de Dios 146

River between the Pongo de Coñeq Canyon and the Pantiacolla anticline, which correspond to 147

the verticalized flanks of the Salvación Syncline (Fig. 1-B). This paper focuses on five 148

selected exposures in cutbanks along the Alto Madre de Dios River. The section includes MD- 149

177, MD-255, MD-256, MD-85 and MD-184 outcrops (Fig. 1-B and Fig. 1-C). Their precise 150

locations are given in the online Supplementary Table A. The five concerned localities yield 151

similar micro- and macrofossils (foraminifers, charophytes, molluscs, ostracods, as well as 152

chondrichthyan and actinopterygian fishes), which allows us to consider them as being time 153

equivalent (Table 1 and Fig. 3). Fifteen sedimentary facies are characterized on the basis of 154

their lithologies, their physical and biogenic sedimentary structures, their palynological and 155

paleontological content, and their geometry (Table 2). For limestone layers of MD-184, 156

standard microfacies descriptions have also been realized. Each of these fifteen facies is 157

interpreted in terms of depositional processes and related depositional environment. On the 158

basis of these interpretations and with regards to the geometrical relationships between the 159

facies, three facies associations are proposed (Table 2). 160

In order to determine the nature of the organic matter (terrestrial versus marine), we 161

analyzed four samples for δ13C TOC content (Table 3) at the NIOZ Institute, Netherlands. The 162

δ13C TOC of higher plants that use the Calvin-Benson cycle of carbon fixation (i.e. so-called C3 163

plants) ranges from -29.3 to -25.5 ‰, with an average value of about -27 ‰ (e.g.  Tyson, 164

1995). The typical marine δ13C CTOC values are in the range of -18 to -22 ‰ (e.g. Meyers, 165

1997). Additional geochemical rock-eval analysis (for sample MD 184) has also been carried 166

out by Repsol Exploration S.A. 167

4. Results 181

4.1. New biostratigraphical and paleoenvironmental constraints from fossil assemblage 182

The fossil content of stratigraphic interest recovered in the studied sections is detailed 184

in the Table 1 and Fig. 3. The concerned material includes vertebrates (chondrichtyans and 185

actinopterygians), ostracods, benthonic foraminifers, and charophytes. Being only recognized 186

at genus, family level, or above, the molluscs found in MD-177, MD-184, and MD-85 are of 187

no use in terms of biostratigraphy (Table 1). Accordingly, MD-177 and MD-184 yielded 188

unidentified Charophyta and Ostracoda. 189

The dominant taxon among vertebrate remains in the concerned deposits is the batoid 190

Ouledia sp. (MD-177; MD-184; MD-85; see Table 1 and Fig. 3 for biostratigraphical results 191

details and Fig. 4 C-D, I-J for an illustration of the key stratigraphic markers). This fossil 192

genus of butterfly rays (gymnurids) is well-known in tropical coastal deposits from Africa and 193

Asia, ranging from the Thanetian up to the Priabonian (Cappetta, 2012). In MD-184, Ouledia 194

is found in association with a pristid sawfish. Pristids are a cosmopolitan family restricted to 195

Cenozoic marine and estuarine localities at world scale (i.e., Danian and onward; Cappetta, 196

2012). In MD-85, Ouledia sp. (mainly represented by worn teeth) co-occurs with Potobatis 197

sp. (Fig. 4 G-H), a dasyatoid stingray so far endemic to Danian marine levels from the top of 198

the El Molino Fm., Bolivia (Cappetta and Gayet, 2013). However, in MD-85, the prismatic 199

teeth referred to as Potobatis sp. are eroded and might have been reworked, which would 200

concur to consider the Danian epoch as a floor age for MD-85. The vertebrate assemblages 201

also include dozens of teeth of an unidentified pycnodontid bony fish (MD-177, MD-184; 202

*Fig. 4 E-F), distinct from but potentially allied to ?Ocloedus toncoensis (Maastrichtian- 203*

Danian of South America; Gonella et al., 2012). Pycnodontids are well represented in 204

Mesozoic and early Paleogene localities, before the family gets extinct during the middle 205

Eocene (Gayet et al., 1993; Poyato-Ariza and Wenz, 2002). 206

Microfossils of high biostratigraphical interest were recovered in MD-255 and MD-85. 207

The agglutinated benthonic foraminifer Karreriella conversa (Eggerellidae), found in MD- 208

255, has an Upper Cretaceous-Lutetian range (Fig. 2; Gradstein et al., 1988; Valchev, 2007). 209

The best constrained locality is MD-85, with a diversified charophyte flora (17 specimens of 210

Peckichara cf. varians meridionalis; 10 specimens of Platychara perlata?; 15 specimens of 211

Feistiella cf. gildemeisteri), the ostracod Protobuntonia sp., and benthonic foraminifers 212

(Reophax sp., Bathysiphon sp., and Rhabdammina sp.). The ostracod Protobuntonia ranges 213

from the Coniacian up to the Thanetian epoch (Morsi et al., 2011); the fragile and delicate 214

valves referred to this taxon in MD-85 are complete (i.e., not likely to be transported or 215

reworked). The charophyte Platychara perlata has a Danian last occurrence in Peru (Sigé et 216

al., 2004). The charophyte Peckichara cf. varians meridionalis is restricted to the 217

Maastrichtian-Thanetian interval (e.g. Musacchio, 1990; Aubry et al., 2005). The charophyte 218

Feistiella cf. gildemeisteri, previously recorded in the Paleocene Yahuarango Formation from 219

Huallaga area, in northern Peru (Hermoza et al., 2005b; Roddaz et al., 2010) and at Laguna 220

Umayo, southern Peru (Jaillard, 1993a), ranges from the Maastrichtian up to the Thanetian or 221

the earliest Ypresian (Sigé et al., 2004; Gelfo et al., 2009; Gelfo and Sigé, 2011; Woodburne et 222

al., 2014). 223

Once combined, all these biostratigraphical data preclude any referral i) to Mesozoic 224

ii) to a post-Paleocene interval (Protobuntonia; Platychara perlata; Peckichara cf. varians 226

meridionalis). In other words, they strongly concur to indicate a Paleocene age for the 227

deposits described in the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (MD-85, MD-177, MD- 228

184, and MD-255 localities; Table 1 and Fig. 3). Yet, based on the biostratigraphical markers 229

4.1.2. Paleoenvironments 244

Thus far, late Cretaceous and Paleocene selachian faunas from Andean and sub- 245

Andean basins consist only of batoids (i.e. no shark is recorded), further known to be highly 246

endemic (de Mowbray and Visser, 1984; Gayet et al., 1993; Cappetta and Gayet, 2013). 247

Together with the complete absence of associated sharks, the co-occurrence of Ouledia (MD- 248

177; MD-184; MD-85), Potobatis (MD-85), two unidentified dasyatoids (MD-177), and a 249

pristid (MD-184) point to shallow waters  in a proximal marine or estuarine environment for 250

the Paleocene deposits described in this study (Cappetta, 2012; Cappetta and Gayet, 2013). 251

The ichthyofauna also includes a high number of pycnodontiform bony fish remains 252

(Pycnodontidae indet.; MD-177; MD-184; MD-85, see Fig. 3 and Fig. 4), some of them being 253

found in partial anatomical connection (i.e., no transport). This extinct group is only recorded 254


<!-- Page 17 -->


14

in marine deposits (shallow water seas; Gayet et al., 1993). However, a freshwater influence is 255

supported by the presence of numerous isolated teeth of characiform bony fishes (MD-177; 256

MD-184; MD-85). Today, characiforms are strictly restricted to freshwaters (Gayet et al., 257

1993). Serrasalmine characiform teeth with a plesiomorphic pattern (Colossoma-like) were in 258

particular recognized in MD-184. 259

The agglutinated foraminifer assemblage, including Karreriella conversa (MD-255), 260

Reophax, Bathysiphon, and Rhabdammina (MD-85), points to a shallow marine inner 261

platform, under unstable environmental conditions, with frequent detrital/terrigenous influxes. 262

Such a continental influence is further attested by the presence of numerous charophyte 263

oogonia (likely to be transported during river flooding episodes) and riverine to brackish 264

molluscs (e.g., Corbicula and Aylacostoma). No open sea indicator, such as dinoflagellates or 265

planktonic foraminifers, has been recorded throughout the sections. 266

To sum up, the macro- and microfossil assemblages (vertebrates, molluscs, ostracods, 267

foraminifers, and charophytes) as documented in MD-177, MD-184, MD-255, and MD-85 268

(Table 1 and Fig. 3) point to an initial idea of the depositional environment: a shallow marine 269

inner platform, under unstable environmental conditions, with frequent detrital/terrigenous 270

5. Depositional environment synthesis 567

Our biostratigraphical results, sedimentary facies interpretations and organic 568

geochemistry analysis indicate the presence of a tide-influenced shallow marine 569

paleoenvironment during the Paleocene in the northern Madre de Dios Basin. Facies 570

association A corresponds to the sedimentary filling of a tide-influenced meandering channel 571

deposited in the fluvial-tidal transition zone. Facies association B corresponds to tidal flats 572

deposits, tidal inlets and also characterizes a tide-influenced environment but with more distal 573

facies than facies association A. Facies association C, interpreted as deposited in a bay/lagoon 574

or stressed shallow marine-environment, is the most distal facies association. The facies of 575

this association do not show any evidence of tidal nor oscillatory currents. 576

The transition between the land and the sea in tide-dominated coastal environments is 577

among the most complex on Earth, because of the interaction of numerous physical, chemical 578

and biological processes (Dalrymple and Choi, 2007). Existing depositional models are 579

therefore preliminary because the number of case studies of many of the subenvironments is 580

rather small (Dalrymple and Choi, 2007). However, our dataset makes the possibility to 581

distinguish between tide-dominated delta and tide-dominated estuary. First, from a geological 582

point of view, estuaries are transgressive whereas deltas are regressive (Dalrymple et al., 583

1992). The tide-dominated Paleocene deposits studied in this paper overly continental 584

deposits of the Yahuarango formation. This stratigraphic succession therefore suggests that the 585

tide-dominated Paleocene deposits are transgressive and related to an estuary. The presence of 586

a Paleocene tide-dominated estuary is further attested by the occurrence of a well expressed 587

tide-influenced meandering zone. According to several works (Dalrymple et al., 1992; 588

Dalrymple and Choi, 2007), only the fluvio-estuarine transition zone in a tide-dominated 589

estuary could explain the occurrence of both opposite currents and meandering channels in a 590

tide-influenced environment. Facies association A could be an illustration of this fluvial-tidal 591

environment, as it shows evidences of meandering channels influenced by both fluvial and 592

tidal currents (Fig. 14). According to this interpretation, Facies association B could be 593

interpreted as deposited in the outer part of this tide-dominated estuary, where tidal inlets are 594

still present and can laterally be connected to muddy and mixed tidal-flat deposits (Fig. 14). 595

Finally, as Facies association C does not show any evidences of tidal currents, we suggest 596

deposition in a shallow confined marine environment (Fig. 14). 597

The data presented in this study document for the first time the existence of Paleocene 599

foreland basin. We favor a Thanetian age for this marine incursion but a Danian age cannot be 601

discarded. Most of Paleocene sedimentary rocks of other parts of the Andean/Amazonian 602

foreland basin were mainly deposited in a distal fluvial environment (see Fig. 2 and 603

references therein). The presence of estuarine deposits overlying continental deposits 604

indicates a marine transgression during the Paleocene. This transgression is caused by an 605

increase in accommodation space which in turn depends on the interplay between sediment 606

supply and base level changes (see Catuneanu, 2004 and references therein). In a retroarc 607

foreland basin setting, numerous mechanisms can be envisaged to account for an increase in 608

accommodation space including eustasy, matle processes, foreland related tectonics (i.e. 609

loading/unloading cycles of (i.e. loading/unloading cycles of Catuneanu et al., 1997) and 610

decrease in sediment supply. The Danian and Thanetian periods are characterized by a drop in 611

global sea-level (Fig. 3) (Haq et al., 1987; Hardenbol et al., 1998; Vandenberghe et al., 2012). 612

Consequently the recorded transgression (Danian or Thanetian in age) is not related at first 613

order to a rise in global sea-level. Dynamic loading may be induced by subduction beneath 614

the retroarc foreland basin. Subduction generates long wavelength subsidence (Mitrovica et 615

al., 1989; Catuneanu et al., 1997; Pysklywec and Mitrovica, 2000; Catuneanu, 2004) capable 616

of maintaining the four depozones of the foreland basin system below the base level 617

(Catuneanu et al., 1997; Catuneanu, 2004) and thus of producing accommodation at the basin 618

scale. In fact, we have no idea of the depositional environment of other depozones (wedgetop, 619

proximal foredeep and backbulge) adjacent to our study area so that it is difficult to exclude 620

subsidence dynamic as a possible mechanism. However, the presence of a Paleocene flexural 621

forebulge in the southern Bolivia foreland basin caused by loading of the Western Cordillera 622

The entrance of this Paleocene marine ingression (Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean or 638

Caribbean Sea) remains to be elucidated. Very few Paleocene marine or coastal deposits are 639

documented in the Andean/Amazonian foreland basins. Paleocene formations of Ecuador and 640

elsewhere in Peru show no evidences of marine or coastal deposits (Fig. 2). In the Bolivian 641

Altiplano and the Eastern Cordillera there is no evidence of any marine influence attested so 642

far except during Danian times in Potosi, Bolivia (El Molino Formation; e.g. Cappetta and 643

Gayet, 2013). Hence the Paleocene paleogeogaphical map proposed here is tentative (Fig. 15- 644

A). In conjunction with the absence of shallow marine deposits in North-western South 645

America, our data might suggest a southern connection with the Atlantic Ocean (Bolivia- 646

Argentina). In any case, more detailed sedimentological works are needed to decipher the 647

Orteguaza and Pozo Formations (Christophoul et al., 2002; Hermoza et al., 2005b; Roddaz et 651

al., 2010). According to these authors, this Eocene marine incursion would come from both 652

the Guyaquil Gulf and the Caribbean Sea (Fig. 15-B). Data from Colombia suggest that a late 653

Eocene transgression flooded south-western Colombia, coming from the south through the 654

Ecuadorian coast (Osorio et al., 2002; Santos et al., 2008). The presence of marine deposits in 655

the Eastern Cordillera and the Central-Eastern Llanos Foothills is more difficult to explain 656

and authors propose a possible corridor through the proto-Lower Magdalena Valley that 657

connected the Caribbean Sea and the Central Llanos Foothills (Santos et al., 2008). In 658

Ecuador and northern Peru, the Eocene shallow marine transgression is recorded by the 659

deposits of Orteguaza and Pozo formation (Fig. 2) as the result of the Western Cordillera 660

The nature of the Andean source (Eastern or Western Cordillera) for the sediments 664

deposited within the Paleocene estuary also remains unclear. Thermochronological evidences 665

suggest that the first exhumation and/or deformation pulse in the eastern part of the Altiplano 666

or in the Eastern Cordillera of Central Andes occurred in the late Eocene (Kontak et al., 1990; 667

Barnes et al., 2006). Jaillard et al. (1993b) interpreted the absence of strata close to the K-Pg 668

boundary in the Cusco basins as the consequence of an uplift of a proto-eastern cordillera 669

occurring as early as the early to late Paleocene. However, provenance data suggest that the 670

Paleocene estuarine sediments studied here are characterized by a contribution from a 671

volcanic arc source. According to Mamani et al. (2010), the only active volcanic arc during 672

related to proto western Cordillera loading. This orogenic loading can be related to a drastic 677

According to the data presented in this study and to literature review, at least two 681

marine incursions occurred in the Amazonian foreland basin in early Paleogene times 682

(Paleocene and Eocene, respectively). Both shallow marine incursions are mainly induced by 683

Andean tectonic loading but they did not affect similar areas in the Amazonian foreland 684

basins. Many studies (see Hoorn et al., 2010) have emphasized the role played by the 685

Miocene long-lived Pebas megawetland system in preventing in situ speciation and floristic 686

and plants dispersal between the Andes and Amazonia for at least 6 Ma (Antonelli et al., 687

2009) and favoring evolutionary transition from marine to freshwater habitats of Neotropical 688

fishes (Lundberg et al., 1998; Lovejoy et al., 2006; 2009). Recurrent Paleogene marine 689

incursions in the Amazonian foreland basin associated with Andean uplift could have 690

provoked biogeographical isolation and promoted allopatric speciation for terrestrial 691

organisms. 692

7. Conclusions 693

Based on a multidisciplinary approach, this paper documents for the first time the 694

presence of a tide-dominated shallow marine paleoenvironment during the Paleocene interval 695

(Danian or Thanetian) in the Amazonian basin. In details, based on sedimentary facies 696

analysis, organic geochemistry and fossil assemblages, three facies associations related to a 697

tide-dominated estuary debouching into a shallow-marine bay or lagoon have been defined. 698

Facies association A corresponds to the sedimentary filling of a tide-influenced meandering 699

channel formed in the fluvial-tidal transition zone. Facies association B is related to more 700

distal tidal-flats, little channelized tidal inlets and saltmarshes deposits. Facies association C 701

corresponds to a stressed shallow marine environment such as a bay or a lagoon. 702

The presence of these transgressive estuarine deposits overlying older continental 703

facies is best explained by flexural tectonic subsidence in response to Andean tectonic 704

loading. This is in agreement with the Nd-Sr isotopic provenance data that show an Andean 705

provenance and hence the presence of an Andean relief during Danian or Thanetian times. 706

The volcanic contribution recorded in the Nd-Sr isotopic compositions can be related to the 707

Toquepala volcanic arc (91 to 45 Ma) located in the present-day Coastal/Western Cordillera. 708

This suggests the absence of any significant proto-Eastern Cordillera relief that would have 709

stopped the drainage and the sedimentary influxes from this Western Andean volcanic relief 710

towards the Amazonian basin during Danian or Thanetian times. Consequently the data 711

suggest that the Danian or Thanetian marine incursion can be related to the subsidence created 712

in response to the proto-Western Cordillera loading. We suggest this Paleocene transgression 713

may come from the south and may be related to the Parana Sea. Finally, similar to Miocene 714

marine incursions affecting the Pebas megawetland, Paleogene marine incursions in the 715

Amazonian foreland basin associated with Andean uplift may have played a role in the 716

dynamics of Neotropical paleobiodiversity in favoring biogeographical isolation and 717

promoting allopatric speciation for terrestrial organisms. 718

## 1. Introduction 48

## The Amazon basin is the world’s largest Cenozoic fluvial basin with an actual drainage 49

area of 5.8×106 km2 and a depositional area of approximately 2.5 to 3×106 km2. The Amazon 50

rainforest, with an area of about 5.6×106 km2, is the largest rainforest ecosystem, representing 51

## nearly 50% of the total tropical rainforest area on Earth. The Amazon rainforest plays a 52

## significant role in global climate, the carbon cycle and biodiversity and is the most species- 53

## rich terrestrial ecosystem in the world. However, the timing of the origin and evolutionary 54

causes of this diversity are still highly debated. A recent synthesis by Hoorn et al. (2010) has 55

## highlighted the complex links between Andean mountain building, climate variability and 56

## biodiversity development throughout Cenozoic times in the Amazonian basin. In particular 57

## the occurrence of inland seaway is important not only in promoting biogeographical isolation 58

## and allopatric speciation but also in controlling the precipitation rates in the Amazon basin 59

## (Jeffery et al., 2012). Consequently, determining the number, timing and duration of Cenozoic 60

## marine incursions recorded in Amazonian basin is fundamental not only for reconstructing 61

## paleo-Amazonian landscapes and ecosystems through time but also for understanding the 62

## close relationships between Andean mountain building and the Cenozoic climate and biotic 63

## evolution of South America. 64

## Several marine incursions have already been described in the Cenozoic sedimentary 65

## record of the Amazonian foreland basins (Roddaz et al., 2010). For instance, the existence and 66

## persistence of the early to middle Miocene Pebas megawetland system in northern Amazonia 67

is thought to have promoted the high biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest (for a review, see 68

(Hoorn et al., 2010) and references therein). However, the extent of this Pebas system and the 69

## number of marine ingressions that have occurred is still under debate (Campbell et al., 2006; 70

Hovikoski et al., 2007; Hoorn et al., 2010) mainly because of poor stratigraphic dating and the 71

## lack of regional data integration. In comparison, few studies document Paleogene marine 72

## incursions in the Amazonian basin. For instance, there is some evidence of a marine 73

## ingression during Eocene to Oligocene times in Colombia (Santos et al., 2008), Ecuador 74

(Christophoul et al., 2002) and northern Peru (Hermoza et al., 2005b), but no data exist for 75

## earlier marine incursions. 76

## In this study, new biostratigraphical, sedimentological and geochemical data are presented to 77

## highlight a Paleocene marine ingression in southern Peru, Madre de Dios basin. A new paleo- 78

## depositional model for these coastal deposits is also proposed. Finally, the paleogeography 79

## and paleo-extension of this shallow marine ingression are discussed. 80

## 2. Geological background 81

### 2.1. Paleocene sedimentary record in the Amazonian foreland basins 82

## In nearly all the Central Andean sedimentary basins, late Eocene to early Oligocene 83

## times are marked by a widespread sedimentary hiatus (Mpodozis and Allmendinger, 1993; 84

## Marocco et al., 1995) corresponding to a major tectonic phase primarily called Incaic 1 phase 85

## (Noble et al., 1990; Jaillard, 1996; Hermoza, 2004). However, there are some localities in 86

## northern and Central Andean foreland basins where Paleocene strata have been preserved and 87

## can be described (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). 88

## In central Colombia, the Cuervos formation is late Paleocene in age (Jaramillo and 89

## Dilcher, 2000; 2001) and its sedimentary rocks correspond to mudstones deposited in a distal 90

alluvial to coastal plain environment, in a foredeep position (Cooper et al., 1995; Parra et al., 91

## 2009). In the Putumayo basin of southern Colombia, the Rumiyaco Formation is barren of 92

fossils and then remains poorly constrained but it is assumed that it is early Paleocene in age. 93

## The Rumiyaco Formation unconformably overlays the Cretaceous series and builts up a 94

## sedimentary wedge onlapping onto older strata and disappearing toward the east of the basin. 95

## The formation is characterized by possibly marine-related to mostly continental fine-grained 96

## deposits in the western part of the Putumayo basin and evolves eastward into continental 97

## sandstones (Bejarano, 1991; Casero, 1997; Córdoba et al., 1997; Londoño et al., 2012). In the 98

## Ecuadorian Oriente basin, Paleocene strata dated by charophytes (Faucher and Savoyat, 1973) 99

## are represented by the deposits of the fluvial Tena Formation. Various studies demonstrated 100

## that sediments from Tena Formation are derived from the Eastern Cordillera of Ecuador (Ruiz 101

## et al., 2004, 2007; Martin-Gombojav and Winkler, 2008). 102

## In Peru, Paleocene strata are very scarce and are only identified in the eastern border 103

## of the Altiplano (Vilquechico Group and Lower Muñani Formation), in the Cusco-Sicuani 104

## 7

## area (Puquin Formation) or in the present-day foreland basin (Yahuarango or Huayabamba 105

## Formations) (Sigé et al., 2004; Gelfo and Sigé, 2011). These strata generally consist of 106

## reddish fine-grained continental deposits and are defined as the Red Beds Formation (Naeser 107

## et al., 1991; Jaillard, 1993a; Hermoza et al., 2005b). The Lower Muñani Formation is dated 108

## 5. Depositional environment synthesis 567

## Our biostratigraphical results, sedimentary facies interpretations and organic 568

## geochemistry analysis indicate the presence of a tide-influenced shallow marine 569

## paleoenvironment during the Paleocene in the northern Madre de Dios Basin. Facies 570

## association A corresponds to the sedimentary filling of a tide-influenced meandering channel 571

## deposited in the fluvial-tidal transition zone. Facies association B corresponds to tidal flats 572

## deposits, tidal inlets and also characterizes a tide-influenced environment but with more distal 573

## facies than facies association A. Facies association C, interpreted as deposited in a bay/lagoon 574

## or stressed shallow marine-environment, is the most distal facies association. The facies of 575

## this association do not show any evidence of tidal nor oscillatory currents. 576

## The transition between the land and the sea in tide-dominated coastal environments is 577

## among the most complex on Earth, because of the interaction of numerous physical, chemical 578

## and biological processes (Dalrymple and Choi, 2007). Existing depositional models are 579

## therefore preliminary because the number of case studies of many of the subenvironments is 580

## rather small (Dalrymple and Choi, 2007). However, our dataset makes the possibility to 581

## distinguish between tide-dominated delta and tide-dominated estuary. First, from a geological 582

## point of view, estuaries are transgressive whereas deltas are regressive (Dalrymple et al., 583

## 1992). The tide-dominated Paleocene deposits studied in this paper overly continental 584

## deposits of the Yahuarango formation. This stratigraphic succession therefore suggests that the 585

## tide-dominated Paleocene deposits are transgressive and related to an estuary. The presence of 586

## a Paleocene tide-dominated estuary is further attested by the occurrence of a well expressed 587

## tide-influenced meandering zone. According to several works (Dalrymple et al., 1992; 588

## Dalrymple and Choi, 2007), only the fluvio-estuarine transition zone in a tide-dominated 589

## estuary could explain the occurrence of both opposite currents and meandering channels in a 590

## tide-influenced environment. Facies association A could be an illustration of this fluvial-tidal 591

## 6. Paleogeographic and tectonic implications 598

## The data presented in this study document for the first time the existence of Paleocene 599

## tide-dominated estuary debouching into a shallow marine bay in the western Amazonian 600

foreland basin. We favor a Thanetian age for this marine incursion but a Danian age cannot be 601

## discarded. Most of Paleocene sedimentary rocks of other parts of the Andean/Amazonian 602

## foreland basin were mainly deposited in a distal fluvial environment (see Fig. 2 and 603

## references therein). The presence of estuarine deposits overlying continental deposits 604

## indicates a marine transgression during the Paleocene. This transgression is caused by an 605

## increase in accommodation space which in turn depends on the interplay between sediment 606

## supply and base level changes (see Catuneanu, 2004 and references therein). In a retroarc 607

## foreland basin setting, numerous mechanisms can be envisaged to account for an increase in 608

## accommodation space including eustasy, matle processes, foreland related tectonics (i.e. 609

## loading/unloading cycles of (i.e. loading/unloading cycles of Catuneanu et al., 1997) and 610

## decrease in sediment supply. The Danian and Thanetian periods are characterized by a drop in 611

global sea-level (Fig. 3) (Haq et al., 1987; Hardenbol et al., 1998; Vandenberghe et al., 2012). 612

## Consequently the recorded transgression (Danian or Thanetian in age) is not related at first 613

## order to a rise in global sea-level. Dynamic loading may be induced by subduction beneath 614

## the retroarc foreland basin. Subduction generates long wavelength subsidence (Mitrovica et 615

## al., 1989; Catuneanu et al., 1997; Pysklywec and Mitrovica, 2000; Catuneanu, 2004) capable 616

## of maintaining the four depozones of the foreland basin system below the base level 617

## (Catuneanu et al., 1997; Catuneanu, 2004) and thus of producing accommodation at the basin 618

## scale. In fact, we have no idea of the depositional environment of other depozones (wedgetop, 619

proximal foredeep and backbulge) adjacent to our study area so that it is difficult to exclude 620

## subsidence dynamic as a possible mechanism. However, the presence of a Paleocene flexural 621

## forebulge in the southern Bolivia foreland basin caused by loading of the Western Cordillera 622

## Based on a multidisciplinary approach, this paper documents for the first time the 694

## presence of a tide-dominated shallow marine paleoenvironment during the Paleocene interval 695

## (Danian or Thanetian) in the Amazonian basin. In details, based on sedimentary facies 696

## stopped the drainage and the sedimentary influxes from this Western Andean volcanic relief 710
